Its quote ends at the corollary's heading, so the card adds the full statement from Appendix B (p12 L54-L61). THM-5's quote begins mid-statement ('T , then with probability ...'); the card adds the theorem's opening with its hypotheses (p7 L4-L13). THM-SMALL-SUPPORT (Corollary 7): the paper gives a one-sentence justification and relies on Corollary 6; Appendix C.2 proves Lemma 4 and Theorem 5 (with Lemmas 9-11) but no proof of Corollary 6 or 7 was found, so it is graded ARGUMENT_ONLY by its weaker part; a reviewer may judge the in-text derivation sufficient for PROVED_IN_PAPER. The debate experiments are called 'proof-of-concept experiments' (p2 L40) and use 100 questions 'due to funding resources'; RES-COMBINED, RES-JUDGE-INDECISION and CORE are graded EMPIRICAL_PRELIMINARY on that basis. CORE mixes a proved algorithmic result and these experiments; its evidence_type is 'theorem' but it is graded by the weaker experimental part.

method.description: Regret bounds for repeated games with N actions are analysed under pure and smooth optimization oracles, a new oracle-based algorithm (Algorithm 1, Theorem 5) minimizes internal and external regret together, and LLM debates on QuALITY-Easy compare noise-injected settings modelling a smooth oracle with a greedy control.

passages.text:
We study efficient regret minimization in large games with access to optimization oracles. We consider
two types of oracles, pure optimization oracles and smooth optimization oracles. A pure optimization
oracle outputs the best response given a set of strategies, and a smooth optimization oracle can
output the best response given noisy feedback. We characterize the external and internal regret of
playing large games with each type of oracle. In particular, we propose an efficient, oracle-based
algorithm for minimizing internal and external regret simultaneously, described in Algorithm 1, and
give its accompanying guarantee in Theorem 5. As far as we know, this is the first oracle-based
method that achieves both external and internal regret, and per-iteration computational complexity
with logarithmic dependence on the size of the action space N . A comparison of our results and
previous methods is given in Table 1.

Finally, we present proof-of-concept experiments in the AI Safety via Debate setting [23]. In AI
Safety via Debate, two AI agents debate a question and a judge must determine which agent provided
a better answer. This model aims to address alignment problems where the agent’s behavior is too
complex for humans to understand without assistance, and it is held that optimal play in this game can
produce aligned and truthful agents. We show that using the insight from our algorithmic analysis,
namely the benefit of a smooth best response oracle, shows clear improvement in gameplay when
applied to the AI Debate setting as compared to the baselines.

stated_hypotheses: Access to an optimization (best-response) oracle; with only a pure oracle, existing lower bounds rule out efficient low-regret algorithms in general, so the efficient results use a smooth (noisy) oracle.
Each oracle call takes unit time.
In the experiments, the expertise gap is simulated by revealing the passage only to the debaters, and debate is treated as a zero-sum game so that external-regret minimization suffices.

Existing lower bounds [21] show that given access to pure optimization oracles, in general we cannot
design efficient algorithms with low regret. We thus consider an augmented oracle: the smooth
optimization oracle.

We assume that a call to an optimization oracle, as defined above, takes unit time. For more discussion
on runtime complexity and efficient representation of mixed strategies, see Appendix A.

Our debate set-up is similar to that of Michael et al. [27], in which two expert debaters assist a
non-expert judge in determining the correct answer to a difficult long-context question-answering
task. We simulate the expertise gap by revealing the passage only to the debaters, whereas the judge
must select an answer using only the debaters’ presented arguments and evidence.
